خصوبتها في السودان بسبب التغير المناخي/ رويترز الدوحة في 01 نوفمبر /قنا/ لم تعد الحرب في السودان وحدها هي ما يشكل تهديدا لحياة السكان؛ فبينما تتواصل المعارك التي مزقت البلاد وأجبرت الملايين على مغادرة منازلهم، يواجه المزارعون هناك عدواً آخر لا تصدر عنه أصوات الرصاص والمدافع، ألا وهو الجفاف الذي قد يدفع السودان مجدداً نحو براثن المجاعة. وفي بلد أنهكته الحرب والنزوح، لم تعد المأساة تختصر في مشهد أرض متشققة تنتظر المطر، ولا في قوافل نازحين يفرون من المعارك؛ فقد زاد الجفاف قساوة المشهد في بلد ظل يوصف بأنه إحدى السلال الغذائية المحتملة للعالم العربي. كما يضيف الجفاف وتقلب الأمطار ضغطاً جديداً على ملايين السودانيين، خصوصاً في الأرياف حيث تعتمد الزراعة والرعي فيها على مواسم المطر. ولا تتوقف تبعات نقص المياه عند الحقول، بل تمتد لتشمل الماشية ومصادر الدخل وقدرة الأسر على تأمين الغذاء الأساسي. ووفق دراسات مناخية، تواجه مناطق زراعية ورعوية في دارفور والنيل الأزرق وسنار والجزيرة تفاوتاً حاداً في الأمطار وتراجعاً في الغطاء النباتي، مما يهدد الإنتاج الزراعي وسبل العيش. وتقول لجنة التصنيف المرحلي المتكامل للأمن الغذائي (وهي مبادرة مدعومة من الأمم المتحدة) إن جفافاً شديداً مرتبطاً بظاهرة النينيو يطال أكثر من نصف مساحة السودان، مما تسبب في فشل محاصيل محلية وحرمان الأسر من الغذاء والدخل. وكانت تقديرات اللجنة في مايو الماضي قد أشارت إلى أن نحو 19.5 مليون شخص، أي أكثر من 40% من السكان، يواجهون مستويات حادة من انعدام الأمن الغذائي. وفي شمال دارفور، أدى تأخر هطول الأمطار وتراجع المخزونات الغذائية إلى مستويات حرجة لتفاقم الأزمة، أما منطقة غرب كردفان فتشهد واحدة من أسوأ موجات الجفاف منذ عام 2004، بحسب معدلات الأمطار المسجلة. وأكدت بيانات دولية أن الأمطار خلال الأشهر الثلاثة الأخيرة، التي تمثل ذروة موسم الأمطار، كانت الأدنى منذ أكثر من ثلاثة عقود في جميع أنحاء السودان. وقد حذرت الأمم المتحدة من أن العجز الشديد في الأمطار يزيد حدة الكارثة الإنسانية، خصوصا في دارفور وأجزاء من كردفان، حيث تضع الحرب السكان أمام صعوبات متزايدة للحصول على الغذاء والمياه والخدمات الصحية. ولا تُعد الزراعة في السودان مجرد قطاع اقتصادي، فقد شكلت عبر أجيال أساساً لحياة ملايين الأسر ومصدراً للغذاء والدخل والاستقرار الاجتماعي. ففي المناطق الريفية، تعتمد عائلات كثيرة على مواسم الأمطار لإنتاج المحاصيل وتوفير العلف للماشية، بينما ترتبط الأسواق المحلية بحركة المزارعين والرعاة والتجار. وهكذا فقد تحولت الأمطار التي ينتظرها المزارعون كل عام إلى مصدر قلق متزايد؛ فالأرض التي يفترض أن تنبت الغذاء والأعلاف فقدت جانباً كبيراً من ريها الطبيعي، والحقول التي نجت من الدمار والنزوح، أصبحت مهددة بتراجع محاصيلها. وفي السياق ذاته، تتقلص قدرة المنظمات الإنسانية على توفير الغذاء للعائلات التي فقدت مصادر رزقها، الأمر الذي يرسم ملامح أزمة ثلاثية الأبعاد تجمع بين الحرب والجفاف ونقص التمويل، وتهدد بتحويل انعدام الأمن الغذائي إلى كارثة أشد خطورة في بلد يعاني بالفعل واحدة من أكبر الأزمات الإنسانية في العالم. وفي بيان أصدرته المنسقة المقيمة ومنسقة الشؤون الإنسانية للأمم المتحدة بالسودان، دينيس براون، في أكتوبر الماضي، حذرت من أن النقص الحاد في الأمطار في بعض المناطق يعمق الأزمة التي يعيشها ملايين السكان. وشددت براون على أن الأطفال الذين تعرضوا بالفعل للنزوح المتكرر يواجهون مخاطر إضافية تتعلق بسوء التغذية والأمراض، وأضافت أن المزارعين أصحاب الحيازات الصغيرة يحتاجون إلى دعم عاجل قبل موسم الزراعة الشتوي. وتعتمد أكثر من 90% من الأراضي الزراعية السودانية على الأمطار، ويقدر مركز الرصد الزراعي الأوروبي الأراضي الزراعية بنحو 206 آلاف كيلومتر مربع، والمراعي بنحو 405 آلاف كيلومتر مربع، من مجموع مساحة السودان المقدرة بنحو 1.86 مليون كيلومتر مربع. ورصد المركز عجزا مطريا خلال ثلاثة أشهر في نحو 196 ألف كيلومتر مربع من الأراضي الزراعية والمراعي النشطة. ويؤدي تراجع الأمطار إلى إبطاء تجدد الأعشاب وتقلص المياه السطحية، مما يضطر الرعاة إلى قطع مسافات أطول بحثا عن الكلأ بسبب نقص المراعي. وقد ينعكس ذلك على إنتاج الألبان واللحوم وأسعار الحيوانات ودخول الأسر، ويزيد التنافس على موارد المياه والمراعي. لكن المناخ ليس الجبهة الوحيدة؛ فالنزاع يقيد وصول المزارعين إلى أراضيهم ويدفعهم إلى النزوح، كما يعطل البنية التحتية وتوافر المدخلات الزراعية، وعندما يتزامن ذلك مع شح المطر، تتراجع قدرة المجتمعات على تعويض خسائر المحاصيل والماشية ويتفاقم انعدام الأمن الغذائي بشكل خطير. ولمعالجة هذه الخسائر، تحتاج الاستجابة الإنسانية إلى إغاثة غذائية عاجلة، وبذور مناسبة للمناخ الجاف، وإعادة تأهيل الآبار والخزانات، وتوفير الأعلاف والخدمات البيطرية، ودعم المزارعين الصغار، وتطوير الري التكميلي وحصاد مياه الأمطار. كما أن فتح الطرق والأسواق وتأمين وصول المزارعين إلى أراضيهم والمساعدات إلى المتضررين يمثل شرطا أساسيا لنجاح التعافي. وقد بلغت الموارد المتاحة لبرنامج الأغذية العالمي لعملياته في السودان نحو 276 مليون دولار حتى 17 أكتوبر 2026، أي أقل من نصف ميزانية العام الماضي، في حين احتاج البرنامج إلى 134 مليون دولار إضافية للتعامل مع الجوع المرتبط بالجفاف، وأدى نقص التمويل إلى خفض الحصص الغذائية التي يوزعها البرنامج في بعض المناطق السودانية إلى النصف تقريبا. وبين أرض تتشقق عطشا، وحقول تنتظر أمطارا لم تأت في موعدها، وملايين أنهكتهم الحرب والنزوح والجوع، يقف السودان أمام أزمة تتجاوز حدود الطقس؛ فالجفاف يبدد أي أمل في التقاط الأنفاس، ويهدد بتعميق خسائر المزارعين والرعاة وتوسيع رقعة الفقر وزيادة الاعتماد على المساعدات، في بلد يملك فعلا موارد زراعية هائلة قادرة على إطعام الملايين لو توفرت لها ظروف نتيقة: 1 نوفمبر 2026: راديو دبنقا تشهد أسواق محلية نتيقة بولاية جنوب دارفور ارتفاعاً في أسعار المحاصيل الزراعية والمواد التموينية، بالتزامن مع تراجع أسعار الماشية، ما فاقم الأوضاع المعيشية للسكان وقلّص قدرتهم على توفير احتياجاتهم اليومية. وبحسب الأسعار المتداولة في الأسواق المحلية، بلغ سعر جوال الدخن 400 ألف، والذرة 380 ألفاً، والفول السوداني 150 ألفاً، فيما وصل سعر جركانة الزيت إلى 300 ألف. كما بلغ سعر عبوة الدقيق زنة 25 كيلوغراماً 175 ألفاً، والأرز 155 ألفاً. وقال المواطن عبد الهادي محمد حامد لراديو دبنقا إن ارتفاع أسعار المحاصيل الزراعية يرتبط بشح الأمطار وفشل الموسم الزراعي في المحلية، مشيراً إلى أن تراجع أسعار الماشية يعود إلى انعدام المراعي وشح الأعشاب، الأمر الذي زاد من معاناة المواطنين وأدى إلى تفاقم الأوضاع الإنسانية. وطالب حامد المنظمات العاملة في المجال الإنساني sudan.summary: شهدت أسواق محلية نتيقة في ولاية جنوب دارفور ارتفاعاً ملحوظاً في أسعار الدقيق والزيت، مما زاد من معاناة السكان. وفقاً للتقارير، بلغ سعر جوال الدخن 400 ألف جنيه، والذرة 380 ألفاً، بينما وصل سعر جركانة الزيت إلى 300 ألف جنيه. كما ارتفعت أسعار المواد الغذائية الأخرى، حيث بلغ سعر عبوة الدقيق زنة 25 كيلوغراماً 175 ألفاً والأرز 155 ألفاً. يُعزى هذا الارتفاع إلى شح الأمطار وفشل الموسم الزراعي، مما أثر سلباً على المحاصيل الزراعية. في المقابل، تراجعت أسعار الماشية بسبب انعدام المراعي، مما زاد من الضغوط الاقتصادية على المواطنين. دعا المواطن عبد الهادي محمد حامد المنظمات الإنسانية إلى التدخل العاجل لتقديم المساعدات اللازمة، لمساعدة السكان في مواجهة الظروف المعيشية الصعبة وتلبية احتياجاتهم الأساسية.

, سنار , كردفان , نهر النيل , ولاية الجزيرة 0 رئاسة محلية الدبة الولاية الشمالية الدبة/ أبو حمد، 1 نوفمبر 2026 – قصفت مسيّرات لقوات الدعم السريع محطتي كهرباء الدبة وأبو حمد شمالي السودان، الأحد، ما تسبب في إخراجهما عن الخدمة. وأكدت مصادر حكومية بمحلية أبو حمد لـ«سودان تربيون» أن مسيّرة استهدفت محطة أبو حمد التحويلية بولاية نهر النيل. كما شمل القصف محطة حرارية قديمة خارج الخدمة كانت في السابق تغذي المدينة. وتسبب القصف في انقطاع الكهرباء في مدينة أبو حمد والقرى المحيطة بها. وفي الولاية الشمالية أفادت مصادر محلية «سودان تربيون» بأن مسيّرة قصفت محطة كهرباء محلية الدبة التحويلية، ما أخرجها عن الخدمة وتسبب في انقطاع التيار عن المدينة وقراها. وطال القصف أيضاً مقار عسكرية بالمدينة، فضلاً عن محطات وقود في منطقة الملتقى التي تبعد حوالي 25 كيلومتراً جنوب شرق مدينة الدبة، ما تسبب في مقتل امرأة قرب إحدى المحطات التي تعرضت للقصف. وتشير «سودان تربيون» إلى أن مسيّرات الدعم السريع قصفت 14 محطة كهرباء خلال أسبوعين في ولايات البحر الأحمر والقضارف ونهر النيل والشمالية والخرطوم والجزيرة وسنار والنيل الأبيض وجنوب كردفان. الكلمات: الدبة، أبو حمد، محطات الكهرباء، انقطاع الكهرباء، الولاية الشمالية، نهر النيل، مسيّرات الدعم السريع، محطات الوقود، الملتقى، الحرب في السودان مقالات ذات صلة الدعم السريع: استسلام جنود مصريون في قاعدة مروي الجوية منحة بـ 100 مليون دولار من البنك الدولي للسودان لمواجهة (كورونا) برلماني سوداني يطالب بالقبض على المصريين حال انتهاء الاقامة البشير يلتقي مبعوثا أمميا قبل المسيّرات في السودان 31 أكتوبر 2026 السودان يطالب المجتمع الدولي بتحمل مسؤولياته تجاه التواطؤ الإثيوبي 31 أكتوبر 2026 الأكثر قراءة هذا الأسبوع السودان يطالب المجتمع الدولي بتحمل مسؤولياته تجاه التواطؤ sudan.summary: أدانت وزارة الخارجية المصرية تصاعد الهجمات بالطائرات المسيرة في السودان، مشيرةً إلى الأثر المدمر لهذه الهجمات على المنشآت المدنية والبنية التحتية، مما أدى إلى سقوط ضحايا بين المدنيين. وأكدت الوزارة أن هذه الهجمات تمثل انتهاكًا صارخًا للقانون الدولي الإنساني، وشددت على ضرورة حماية المدنيين وتجنب تعريضهم للخطر. كما أعربت مصر عن رفضها لكافة أشكال العنف ضد الأبرياء، ودعت إلى وقف تدفق الأسلحة إلى قوات الدعم السريع من الدول المجاورة. وأكدت على دعمها لوحدة السودان وسيادته، مشددةً على أهمية احترام دول الجوار لسيادة السودان وعدم التدخل في شؤونه الداخلية. وطالبت مصر بتكثيف الجهود الإقليمية والدولية للتوصل إلى وقف إطلاق النار وضمان وصول المساعدات الإنسانية، مع ضرورة تهيئة الظروف لتحقيق تسوية سياسية شاملة تلبي تطلعات الشعب السوداني في الأمن والاستقرار.

أضرار في محطة المرخيات للطاقة شمال أم درمان جراء هجوم نُسب إلى قوات الدعم السريع (الفرنسية) استمع 4:44 0:00 4:44 2:02 ملخص المقال المزيد من التفاصيل استهدفت طائرات مسيّرة محطتي كهرباء أبو حمد والدبة شمالي السودان، مما تسبب في اشتعال النيران بإحداهما. ارتفع عدد محطات الكهرباء المستهدفة بمسيرات في عدة ولايات سودانية إلى 13 محطة خلال أسبوع. استهدفت طائرة مسيّرة، فجر اليوم الأحد، محطة كهرباء أبو حمد في ولاية نهر النيل شمالي السودان ، مما أدى إلى اندلاع حريق فيها، وفق شهود عيان، إضافة إلى استهداف محطة كهرباء الدبة بالولاية الشمالية، وفق ما أفاد مراسل الجزيرة نت. وبذلك يرتفع عدد محطات الكهرباء التي تعرضت لهجمات بطائرات مسيرة في السودان إلى 13 منذ الاثنين الماضي، في ولايات الخرطوم والجزيرة وسنار والقضارف ونهر النيل والبحر الأحمر . أخبار مقترحة غوتيريش يندد بمقتل مئات المدنيين في هجمات المسيّرات بالسودان على حدود تشاد.. نازحو دارفور يفرون بلا ماء بعد سيطرة الدعم السريع على الآبار وأفاد شهود عيان لوكالة الأناضول بأن طائرة مسيرة قصفت، فجر اليوم، محطة كهرباء أبو حمد التحويلية، مما تسبب في اشتعال النيران فيها. وأضاف الشهود أن القصف ترافق مع دوي انفجارات قوية في المنطقة الواقعة فيها المحطة بمدينة أبو حمد التي تبعد نحو 538 كيلومترا عن العاصمة الخرطوم. وتداول ناشطون على مواقع التواصل الاجتماعي مقاطع فيديو تُظهر اشتعال النيران في المحطة. وتمثلت آخر الهجمات على محطات الكهرباء بالسودان، قبل هجوم اليوم الأحد، في استهداف طائرة مسيّرة، أمس السبت، محطة كهرباء هيا بولاية البحر الأحمر شرقي البلاد، أبريل/نيسان 2023، يخوض الجيش السوداني وقوات الدعم السريع حربا اندلعت إثر خلافات بشأن توحيد المؤسسة العسكرية، وأسفرت عن مقتل عشرات الآلاف ونزوح نحو 13 مليون شخص، وسط تفاقم المجاعة والأزمة الإنسانية في 2026-وسائل التواصل شمال السودان – 1 نوفمبر 2026 – راديو دبنقا تعرضت محطة كهرباء مدينة أبو حمد بولاية نهر النيل لهجوم بطائرات مسيرة فجر اليوم الأحد، كما تعرضت محطة كهرباء الدبة في الولاية الشمالية لهجوم مماثل، بجانب هجوم على موقع عسكري بالمدينة. وقال شهود عيان من مدينة أبو حمد إنهم سمعوا ثلاثة انفجارات، مشيرين إلى أن الهجوم استهدف محطة أبو حمد للكهرباء؛ ما أدى لانقطاع التيار الكهربائي في المدينة. وفي الولاية الشمالية، أفادت مصادر بأن مسيرة تتبع للدعم السريع استهدفت محطة الكهرباء الرئيسية في الدبة بالولاية الشمالية. وأدى الهجوم إلى خروج محطة كهرباء مدينة الدبة عن الخدمة وانقطاع التيار الكهربائي. كما استهدف الهجوم مقر قيادة اللواء (73) مشاة ومحطتين للوقود بمنطقة “المتلقى” بالولاية الشمالية، وتسبب في سقوط قتلى وجرحى، من بينهم قائد كتيبة البراء بن مالك المساندة للجيش في الدبة، محمد النو. وبلغ عدد محطات الكهرباء التي تعرضت للهجوم خلال أسبوع (10) محطات؛ ما أدى لانقطاع التيار الكهربائي عن أجزاء واسعة من البلاد. من جانبها، أدانت لجان مقاومة دنقلا الهجوم على محلية الدبة بالولاية الشمالية، والذي طال محطات الكهرباء؛ مما أدى إلى انقطاع التيار الكهربائي بشكل كامل عن المنطقة، وإلحاق أضرار جسيمة بممتلكات المواطنين ومرافق الخدمات الأساسية. وطالبت بالإدانة الفورية لهذه الجريمة التي تستهدف المدنيين والبنية التحتية، والتدخل العاجل من المنظمات الإنسانية والحقوقية لتوثيق هذه الانتهاكات، وتقديم الدعم اللازم لإعادة التيار الكهربائي للمواطنين، وتحييد المرافق المدنية والبنية التحتية عن الصراع المسلح، ووقف الاستهداف العشوائي للمناطق التي يوجد بها مدنيون. غوتيريش أعادت الأمم المتحدة دق ناقوس الخطر حيال التحول المتسارع للطائرات المسيّرة إلى أداة رئيسية لقتل المدنيين وتدمير مقومات الحياة في السودان، بعدما عبّر الأمين العام أنطونيو غوتيريش عن صدمته من الحصيلة الكارثية للهجمات التي ينفذها طرفا الحرب. وقال المتحدث باسم الأمين العام، ستيفان دوجاريك ، في بيان صدر في نيويورك ، إن غوتيريش يشعر بالفزع إزاء تصاعد هجمات المسيّرات وما تخلّفه من خسائر فادحة بين المدنيين، بمن فيهم النساء والأطفال، في أنحاء السودان ومنطقة أبيي. وأدان غوتيريش الهجمات التي تستهدف المدنيين والمنشآت الحيوية، بما فيها المرافق الصحية، مؤكداً أنها قد تمثل انتهاكات للقانون الدولي الإنساني. ودعا الجيش السوداني وقوات الدعم السريع إلى حماية السكان والبنية التحتية المدنية والاتفاق، من دون تأخير، على وقف الأعمال العدائية تمهيداً لإنهاء الحرب. المسيّرات تتصدر أسباب قتل المدنيين يأتي الموقف الأممي بعدما تحولت المسيّرات من سلاح يستهدف المواقع العسكرية وخطوط الإمداد إلى مصدر رئيسي للخسائر المدنية خلال عام 2026، مع اتساع استخدامها لضرب الأسواق وملاجئ النازحين والمستشفيات ومحطات الكهرباء والمياه والوقود. وكانت مفوضية الأمم المتحدة لحقوق الإنسان قد وثقت مقتل 306 أشخاص وإصابة المئات بالمسيّرات خلال 3 أسابيع فقط من أكتوبر. وقالت الأمم المتحدة لاحقاً إن هذه الهجمات أصبحت السبب الأول للوفيات المدنية المرتبطة بالحرب خلال العام. وأكدت وكيلة الأمين العام للشؤون السياسية روزماري ديكارلو أمام مجلس الأمن أن الضربات الجوية وهجمات المسيّرات تعرض المدنيين للخطر في مختلف أنحاء السودان، ودعت الطرفين إلى وقف استخدامها فوراً، أو الاتفاق في الحد الأدنى على ترتيبات عملية صارمة تمنع توجيهها نحو التجمعات والمرافق المدنية. وشهدت مدينة نيالا واحدة من أكثر الهجمات دموية، عندما استُهدف سوق تنقونج في 26 أكتوبر بضربة نسبتها منظمات إنسانية وحقوقية إلى القوات المسلحة السودانية. وقالت مجموعة "محامو الطوارئ" إن الهجوم قتل 102 مدني وأصاب 113 آخرين، بينهم نساء وأطفال. كما اتُّهم الجيش بتنفيذ ضربات على ملاجئ للنازحين وأسواق ومناطق مأهولة في دارفور وكردفان، بينما نُسبت إلى قوات الدعم السريع هجمات متزامنة على محطات الكهرباء والوقود والمياه في الولايات الخاضعة لسيطرة الجيش. وتكشف هذه الوقائع أن امتلاك الطرفين مسيّرات بعيدة المدى لم يحقق حسماً عسكرياً، بل وسّع رقعة الحرب وأدخل المدن البعيدة عن خطوط المواجهة المباشرة في دائرة القصف وانقطاع الخدمات. السودان في دائرة الخطر الحرج Published 13 hours ago on November 1, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk A speaker reads a statement alongside two other men during an apparent Alliance for Survival press briefing. Photo credit: TMC/ Screenshot & Illustrated by Kulu Media The Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, a coalition of armed and political opposition groups, has issued a new statement calling for coordinated action against Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and outlining its position on Ethiopia’s political and security crises. In a four-page statement dated October 31, 2026, and shared on Facebook , the coalition, also known as the Alliance for Survival, accused the federal government of deepening the country’s political divisions, prolonging armed conflicts and failing to protect civilians. The alliance argued that Ethiopia’s current challenges require fundamental political change rather than measures undertaken by the existing administration. It presented cooperation among opposition organizations and communities as central to achieving that objective. The statement blamed the government for what the coalition described as widespread insecurity, displacement, human rights violations and deteriorating economic conditions. These allegations represent the alliance’s position and have not all been independently verified. The coalition also reiterated its opposition to the current federal administration and emphasized the need for a political arrangement that would protect the rights, security and participation of Ethiopia’s different communities. Its statement called for broader cooperation among political organizations, community representatives and other groups opposed to the government. It also addressed members of Ethiopia’s security institutions, urging them to reconsider their role in the country’s political and military conflicts. The alliance has previously identified the replacement of the current government and the establishment of an inclusive transitional administration as central objectives. The latest declaration continues that political position, although it does not establish that a transition has been agreed upon or that the coalition has secured additional territory or military support. The Alliance for Survival emerged in September 2026 as a coalition bringing together organizations with different political backgrounds and regional interests, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Oromo Liberation Army. Its formation drew attention because some participating organizations have historically pursued competing political objectives or fought on opposing sides of earlier conflicts. Their cooperation reflects a shared opposition to the federal government, but does not necessarily mean that their wider political differences have been resolved. The new statement comes amid renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia, including confrontations involving TPLF-aligned forces, the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) and the Tigray Peace Force (TPF). Recent developments in Tigray have included the reported reentry of TPLF forces into Rama , followed by reports of drone strike damage in the area . The conflict has raised questions about the alliance’s military coordination and the extent to which its members can pursue a common strategy despite their differing political priorities. The declaration appears intended to reaffirm the coalition’s continued political cooperation and appeal for wider support. However, the statement does not independently establish a new joint military offensive, a formal agreement with additional organizations or a change in the balance of forces on the ground. No new response from the Ethiopian federal government to the October 31 statement had been independently verified at the time of writing. The alliance’s declaration adds to the political uncertainty surrounding Ethiopia’s continuing conflicts, although the practical implications of its latest calls remain unclear. Addressing the Third Russia–Africa Summit in Moscow, Abiy said the proposed Ethiopia nuclear power plant would diversify the country’s electricity supply, which currently relies heavily on hydropower. “With Russia, we are moving toward our first nuclear power plant in line with the safety standards of the International Atomic Energy Agency,” Abiy said in his summit speech , published on his official YouTube channel. The prime minister said nuclear technology could also help reduce agricultural food losses and support healthcare, including cancer treatment. He emphasized that cooperation with Moscow should develop Ethiopian expertise to operate and regulate nuclear facilities. The remarks come as Ethiopia seeks to diversify its electricity generation beyond hydropower, which remains vulnerable to variations in rainfall and reservoir inflows. Earlier this year, Ethiopian Electric Power reported a 20 percent reduction in water inflows linked to El Niño conditions, prompting revisions to its electricity generation and revenue targets. Ethiopia’s nuclear ambitions have been under development for several years. The country signed an intergovernmental nuclear cooperation agreement with Russia in 2019, followed by additional cooperation roadmaps. In March 2026, the Ethiopian Nuclear Energy Commission and Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom signed a strategic roadmap covering nuclear energy development. According to World Nuclear News, Ethiopia is considering two reactors with a combined generating capacity of approximately 2,400 megawatts. However, the project remains at the planning stage, with potential sites requiring further assessment. Abiy did not announce a construction start date, final financing agreement or completion timetable during his Moscow address. The prime minister identified food security, energy and knowledge as Ethiopia’s three principal development priorities. On agriculture, he called for Russian cooperation in farm machinery and agricultural processing industries to increase domestic production and strengthen food security. He said Ethiopia wanted to move beyond producing raw agricultural commodities by expanding industries capable of processing harvested products. Abiy also announced that Ethiopia is establishing the Medemer University of Artificial Intelligence in Addis Ababa and invited Russian universities and research institutions to participate in teaching and research. “An African researcher should be able to create tools in the language of our people,” he said, emphasizing that African institutions should determine how artificial intelligence systems use their data. The proposed university forms part of Ethiopia’s broader technological development ambitions. At the recent Tana High-Level Forum, Abiy also outlined the country’s Digital Ethiopia 2030 strategy , highlighting digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence and data governance as priorities for economic development. The prime minister said scientific cooperation should produce practical economic benefits rather than remain limited to academic exchanges. He invited Russian enterprises to establish joint ventures in Ethiopia’s special economic zones, particularly in pharmaceutical manufacturing and machinery production. Such investments, he said, could supply markets across Africa through the African Continental Free Trade Area. Abiy also called for improved payment arrangements between Ethiopia and Russia to make bilateral trade simpler and less expensive. His proposals came as the two countries continued expanding diplomatic, economic and military cooperation. During the Moscow summit, Abiy held bilateral discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin on nuclear energy, healthcare, trade and other areas of mutual interest. The talks followed Ethiopia’s recent announcement concerning the acquisition of Russian military aircraft and air-defence equipment. On October 28, Kulu Media reported that Ethiopia announced new Russian Su-35 fighter jets amid renewed military tensions in the Horn of Africa. The latest summit discussions indicate that Ethiopia is seeking cooperation with Moscow across both civilian and defence sectors. Abiy also proposed that Addis Ababa host a future Russia–Africa Summit when the gathering next takes place on the African continent. He said the Ethiopian capital, which hosts the African Union headquarters, would be honored to welcome the meeting. However, he did not announce that Addis Ababa had been formally selected as the venue. The prime minister urged participating countries to adopt an action plan containing clear responsibilities and implementation timelines. He said international cooperation should translate diplomatic commitments into practical results. On international affairs, Abiy reaffirmed Ethiopia’s support for negotiated solutions, African-led mediation and consistent application of the United Nations Charter. His remarks came amid continuing Ethiopia-Eritrea tensions , with international partners urging restraint and diplomatic engagement to prevent a broader regional conflict. Abiy did not directly address the dispute with Eritrea in the supplied summit speech. Reflecting on historical relations, the prime minister recalled a Russian medical mission that assisted wounded Ethiopians following the Battle of Adwa in 1896. He said the mission translated a medical guide into Amharic, presenting the initiative as an early example of scientific cooperation between the two countries. Abiy also noted that his book Medemer had been translated into Russian, describing the exchange of knowledge as a symbol of the longstanding relationship. The speech concluded with a call for stronger cooperation based on sovereignty, technological capability and shared economic development. For Ethiopia, the proposed nuclear power plant, artificial intelligence university and expanded industrial partnerships represent central elements of the government’s long-term development agenda. However, the financing, construction timetable and implementation arrangements for the nuclear project remain to be finalized. Photo Credit: PM Abiy Ahmed Ali/Facebook Ethiopia has announced the arrival of 12 advanced Russian Su-35 fighter jets, marking a major expansion of its military airpower as renewed fighting in Tigray and worsening relations with Eritrea raise security concerns across the Horn of Africa. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced the delivery on October 28, 2026, saying the aircraft were supplied under an existing defence agreement with Russia. He also confirmed plans for Ethiopia to receive four batteries of Russia’s S-400 air-defence system, although no delivery date was announced. According to Ethiopia’s state-affiliated Fana Media Corporation , Abiy described the arrival of the aircraft as an important step in strengthening national security and protecting Ethiopia’s sovereignty. The prime minister said Russian President Vladimir Putin had helped accelerate the delivery, allowing Ethiopia to receive the fighter jets one year earlier than originally scheduled. The announcement coincided with Abiy’s visit to Russia for the third Russia–Africa Summit, where defence cooperation has become a prominent element of relations between Addis Ababa and Moscow. The Su-35 is a Russian-built, twin-engine multirole fighter aircraft designed for air-to-air combat and air-to-ground missions. Its advanced radar, maneuverability and weapons capabilities could expand the Ethiopian Air Force’s operational options. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Ethiopian and Russian officials pose for a group photograph in front of a fighter aircraft during a military aviation event. Photo Credit: PM Abiy Ahmed Ali / Facebook The planned S-400 acquisition would add another dimension to Ethiopia’s military modernization. The Russian-developed system is designed to detect and engage aircraft, missiles and other airborne threats at considerable distances. However, the government has not disclosed the value of the agreement, the expected arrival date of the S-400 batteries or where the newly acquired aircraft will be stationed. In its October 28 report , Reuters said Russian state-owned defence conglomerate Rostec had not immediately responded to a request for comment. The aircraft delivery announcement comes during a particularly sensitive period for Ethiopia’s security environment. Fighting involving the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF), TPLF-aligned forces and the Tigray Peace Force (TPF) has intensified in northern Ethiopia since September, while relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara have deteriorated sharply. The Ethiopian government has accused Eritrea of supporting TPLF-aligned forces and interfering in Ethiopia’s internal security affairs. Eritrea has rejected accusations of involvement and has made counterclaims concerning Ethiopian military intentions. Earlier this month, Ethiopia formally accused Eritrea of an invasion , alleging that Eritrean troops had advanced into northern Ethiopia. The allegations remain disputed. Ethiopian military chief Field Marshal Berhanu Jula also recently accused Eritrea, Egypt and Sudan of supporting TPLF-aligned forces, including through alleged weapons transfers. Those specific allegations have not been independently verified. The new aircraft could strengthen Ethiopia’s capacity to defend its airspace and conduct military operations, although their immediate operational readiness and deployment arrangements remain unknown. There is no verified evidence that the newly delivered Su-35 fighters have been deployed in the current fighting or assigned to operations against Eritrea. The acquisition nevertheless carries regional significance because Ethiopia and Eritrea remain locked in a confrontation involving border security, political alliances and Ethiopia’s long-standing interest in reliable access to the Red Sea. International concern about a broader conflict has increased. The United States recently warned of wider war , urging restraint as tensions between the two countries continued. Russia has also indicated a willingness to facilitate discussions between Ethiopia and Eritrea if both governments agree, but no confirmed bilateral negotiations have emerged from the Moscow summit. Ethiopia and Russia have maintained military relations for decades, including cooperation involving combat aircraft, defence equipment and technical training. The latest announcement signals a further strengthening of those ties at a time when Ethiopia is seeking to modernize its armed forces while navigating internal conflict and regional diplomatic pressure. For now, the confirmed government announcement concerns the delivery of 12 Su-35 fighter jets. The four S-400 air-defence batteries remain part of a future delivery commitment, with their schedule and deployment locations undisclosed. Photos shared by him on social media show him taking part in military exercises alongside ministers, deputy ministers and heads of government institutions at the Hurso military training centre. The move is unusual in Ethiopia, where senior civilian government officials are rarely seen undergoing military training. Those taking part include Speaker of the House of Federation Muferiat Kamil, Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba. It is unclear when the training began or how long it is expected to last. In his post, the prime minister, who is known as Abiy, said Ethiopia's ambition to achieve universal prosperity required its leadership to be physically fit, morally strong and intellectually capable. He said military institutions offered valuable lessons in discipline, patriotism, teamwork, accountability and leadership. "Soldiers have targets while civilians have goals. The objective of both is victory," he said, adding that combining military and civilian disciplines would help create a generation capable of achieving both. Abiy argued that military training could help develop leaders with a strong sense of purpose, responsibility and the ability to work together towards common objectives. The training comes as Ethiopia faces multiple security challenges, including continued fighting in parts of the northern Tigray region, conflict in Amhara and insecurity in Oromia. It also takes place amid heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, with concerns over the possibility of renewed conflict between the two countries. Abiy has previously emphasised military preparedness and national development as central to his government's ambitions. Opposition Parties, UN Agencies Sound Alarm Over Security Incidents, Civilian Safety in Ethiopia 3 minute read By Abraham Tekle October 31, 2026 Share Facebook X WhatsApp Linkedin Email Telegram Copy URL UN agencies report tens of thousands fled to Kenya Opposition political parties and United Nations agencies have voiced mounting concern over civilian casualties, security incidents, and displacement across parts of Ethiopia, urging immediate measures to protect citizens, investigate reported violations, and ensure accountability amid ongoing regional violence. The Ethiopian Citizens for Social Justice (EZEMA), in a statement issued on October 27, expressed concern that the government has fallen short of its primary obligation to ensure public safety. EZEMA also criticized public media outlets, including the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC), for omitting reports of civilian casualties following incidents in the Arsi Zone of the Oromia Region earlier in the month. Detailing multiple security challenges, the party noted that violence in Arsi, alongside recurring inter-communal clashes in the past months in Gambella and Moyale, has led to loss of life, displacement, and property damage. EZEMA called on federal authorities to take proactive steps to prevent further escalations, transparently investigate institutional shortcomings, and hold responsible parties accountable. Furthermore, the party urged human rights organizations to independently examine the incidents and called for greater public media scrutiny regarding the government’s crisis response. The party appealed to federal and regional authorities to thoroughly investigate the violations, safeguard civilians, and prosecute perpetrators regardless of their official standing or political affiliation. It also encouraged international organizations, diplomatic missions, and human rights monitors to closely follow the situation, cautioning that it is prepared to organize peaceful public demonstrations under the slogan ‘Beka!’ (Enough!) if its demands for security and accountability remains unmet. Echoing these concerns, the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Party (EPRP) issued a statement condemning killings, abductions, and forced displacements in the Arsi Zone, specifically highlighting Shirka and Chole districts. Citing local information, the party reported multiple deaths, injuries, and the alleged abduction of approximately 50 individuals from their homes. The EPRP advocated for an independent international investigation, the safe release of abducted persons, humanitarian assistance for displaced populations, and legal action against those culpable. These developments align with findings from the Ethiopian Human Rights Council (EHRCO), which documented a pattern of killings, injuries, abductions, and displacement across Oromia, Amhara, Gambella, and Benishangul-Gumuz in its annual human rights report covering June 2025 to June 2026. The council reiterated calls for regional and federal authorities to prioritize civilian protection and comprehensive investigations. From The Reporter Magazine From Unwilling Investors to Bidding Wars: Ethiopia’s T-Bill Market Turns on Its Head Published on 2026-09-03 By Mahlet Mehdi Washington Has Sent a Sufficient Signal to PM Abiy on Military Operations: Ex-CIA Analyst Published on 2026-09-28 By Bewket Abebe Behind Ethiopia’s Stalled Iron Ore Mining Published on 2026-08-29 By Bewket Abebe Cities as Engines of Growth and Nation-Building: Reframing Urbanization Discourses in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) Published on 2026-09-14 By Mussie Delelegn Arega (PhD) While accountability for specific incidents remains heavily contested, Oromia Regional Government Communication Bureau Head Hailu Adugna characterized recent violence in the region as an attempt by an armed group referring to itself as ‘Tsmido’ to ignite ethnic and religious strife. Tsimdo refers to armed forces who claims to forge alliance against the government. Hailu expressed deep regret over the loss of lives and material damage resulting from the unrest. Concurrently, reports of active conflict and civilian casualties have emerged from the Amhara and Tigray regions. International media reported that drone strikes hit the Jari No. 2 displacement camp in the South Wollo Zone of the Amhara Region, resulting in a reported death toll including children—alongside numerous injuries requiring hospitalization. In the Tigray Region of Rama town, local residents reported a separate strike affecting a truck transporting sorghum, causing casualties among individuals gathered at the scene. Additional reports from October detailed airstrikes and drone activity in Adwa, Shire, and Sheraro, resulting in civilian deaths and damage to local infrastructure. The impact of the ongoing security challenges has also spilled across international borders. According to the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR), clashes near the Ethiopian-Kenyan border have prompted thousands to cross into Kenya via Moyale since October 22. Local authorities estimate that up to 50,000 individuals have crossed, with registration and verification efforts ongoing. Many of those fleeing are women and children, finding temporary shelter in local schools, churches, or with host communities. In response, the UNHCR, alongside the International Organization for Migration (IOM), UNICEF, and the World Food Programme, has launched an appeal for USD8.9 million to provide essential humanitarian assistance to up to 50,000 displaced individuals over a three-month period. The IOM indicated that humanitarian partners are actively preparing for further arrivals. Addressing the broader climate of conflict, UN Secretary-General António Guterres emphasized in a public statement that adherence to international law, addressing root causes, and pursuing political settlements remain the only viable pathways to sustainable peace. “Let’s summon the political will to silence the guns, stop the killing, and build a world where peace for all prevails,” he stated. From the Cradle of the Nile: Ethiopia’s Sea-Access Ambitions Take Center Stage at Tana 10 minute read By Ashenafi Endale October 31, 2026 Share Facebook X WhatsApp Linkedin Email Telegram Copy URL Sitting on the southern shores of Lake Tana—the mystical, sprawling cradle of the Blue Nile—Bahir Dar offers a striking, almost poetic metaphor for the turbulence currently gripping the Horn of Africa and the wider continent. The Nile has long flowed as the lifeblood of East and North African hydropolitics, binding nations together in an inescapable web of shared geography, competing ambitions, and intense historical rivalry. It was precisely within this metaphorical watershed that policymakers, regional leaders, senior military commanders, and prominent researchers gathered for the 12th Edition of the Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa. Returning after a hiatus forced by escalating regional conflicts, the 2026 summit convened under the sharp, pragmatic theme dubbed ‘Pathways to Peace in Africa: Economic Sovereignty and Geopolitical Transformation.’ Yet, while official panel sessions wrestled with the high-minded mechanics of continental trade integration, digital imperialism, monetary frameworks, and macroeconomic governance, the dominant pulse of the conference floor belonged to an unyielding national imperative. Ethiopia’s bold, unapologetic push for reliable, sovereign sea access, set against a backdrop of deep continental fragmentation, the ravages of conflict economies in Sudan and the Sahel, and the urgent demand for structural self-reliance. The deep symbolism of the host city itself exerts its own weigh on the debates that unfolded in Bahirdar. Lake Tana is not merely a geographical landmark; it is the origin point of the Blue Nile, a river that sustains millions downstream while fueling a century-old geopolitical contest over water security, sovereignty, and regional hegemony. In this light, hosting a premier security summit dedicated to economic sovereignty and geopolitical transformation on the very banks of the Nile is deeply profound. From The Reporter Magazine Drought Emergency or Seasonal Deficit ? Published on 2026-09-02 By The Reporter Magazine What the Old Developmental State Got Wrong Published on 2026-10-02 By Samson Berhane 25-Year Sentences & Retroactive Laws: Controversial Draft Law Sparks Fears of Growing Authoritarianism in Tigray Published on 2026-06-21 By Yared Nigussie Red Sea Rivalries: What a Shifting Geopolitical Landscape Means for Ethiopia and The Horn Published on 2026-08-31 By Yared Nigussie East Africa’s enduring hydropolitical tension is mirrored by Ethiopia’s modern strategic dilemma. A nation of over 130 million people, locked behind borders drawn by historical compromises, is seeking a permanent economic outlet to the world. This geographic vulnerability forms the crucible in which Ethiopia’s current foreign policy is forged. When PM Abiy Ahmed took the podium to open the summit, he did not shy away from the persisting core structural realities. Urging African states to shape rather than merely adapt to global power shifts, Abiy placed sovereignty at the center of the continental dialogue, declaring that Africa must stop being a passive recipient of external prescriptions and instead author its own destiny. “By combining its capacities and developing solutions suited to its own realities, Africa can strengthen its role in shaping the global order and securing a better future for generations to come,” Abiy noted, stressing that homegrown solutions are non-negotiable for lasting stability. From The Reporter Magazine From Unwilling Investors to Bidding Wars: Ethiopia’s T-Bill Market Turns on Its Head Published on 2026-09-03 By Mahlet Mehdi Washington Has Sent a Sufficient Signal to PM Abiy on Military Operations: Ex-CIA Analyst Published on 2026-09-28 By Bewket Abebe Behind Ethiopia’s Stalled Iron Ore Mining Published on 2026-08-29 By Bewket Abebe Cities as Engines of Growth and Nation-Building: Reframing Urbanization Discourses in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) Published on 2026-09-14 By Mussie Delelegn Arega (PhD) Crucially, anchoring this push for strategic autonomy, Ethiopian leadership articulated the core national doctrine that secure, unfettered access to the sea is an existential necessity for a growing population of over 130 million, rather than a negotiable diplomatic luxury or a casual geopolitical preference. That message was echoed with striking, unvarnished directness by Ethiopia’s top security and defense leadership. Redwan Hussein, director general of Information Network Security Administration (INSA) and Field Marshal Berhanu Jula, Chief of Staff of Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF), underscored during the deliberations that Ethiopia’s national interest in maritime access, framing it not as an aggressive encroachment on neighbors, but as a vital economic lifeline required to prevent structural strangulation and ensure long-term regional stability. However, behind closed doors, in the academic corridors, and among international policy observers, this rhetoric met with analytical scrutiny. Regional and international scholars immediately posed the hard, skeptical question of whether Ethiopian officials are simply staking out a long-term bargaining position to secure alternative port arrangements in a volatile neighborhood, or if there is a tangible, realistic, and peaceful roadmap on the table. Critics note that while the rallying national agenda of maritime rights galvanizes domestic political consensus, navigating the hostile geopolitical realignments of the Red Sea basin demands far more than political will. With the Horn of Africa caught in a web of shifting alliances—marked by friction between Asmara, Cairo, Port Sudan, and Mogadishu, alongside mounting Middle Eastern proxy interventions—analysts warn that uncalibrated maritime ambitions risk inflaming already volatile fault lines unless backed by transparent, cooperative diplomatic frameworks. Presenters and researchers also emphasized that maritime access cannot be separated from the broader architecture of regional trust, arguing that any sustainable framework must reconcile Ethiopia’s legitimate economic needs with the sovereignty and security concerns of neighboring littoral states. The urgency of Ethiopia’s national posture played out against the grim, comprehensive diagnosis detailed in the Tana Secretariat’s official State of Peace and Security in Africa Report, which was presented to the delegates by Tana Board Chairperson and former Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama. The report paints a sobering, data-driven picture of a continent grappling with the dangerous regionalization of violence, the institutionalization of conflict economies, and the erosion of multilateral mediation. Nowhere was this regional contagion more pronounced than in the ongoing catastrophe in Sudan. According to the report’s two-phase analysis covering January 2025 to June 2026, the war underwent a qualitative shift following RSF’s capture of El Fasher, cementing the country’s complete territorial and political fragmentation, with the RSF controlling western gold corridors and the Sudanese Armed Forces holding Khartoum and eastern red sea routes. Panelists detailed how the conflict is sustained by the direct and indirect commodification of violence, where illicit gold trade funnels upwards of USD400 million annually into war chests, financing recruitment, weaponry, and the proliferating use of drones. This internal war has inevitably spilled across borders, drawing in Chad, South Sudan, Egypt, Ethiopia, and proximate Gulf powers, transforming the wider region into a theater of competing middle-power rivalries. Mahama himself underscored the human cost of these dynamics, warning the assembly that Africa cannot achieve economic sovereignty while entire populations are displaced and state institutions collapse under the weight of resource-driven civil wars. The summit also turned a critical eye toward the intractable crises in the eastern DRC, where despite diplomatic milestones like the Declaration of Principles and the Washington Accord, fighting between M23 and government forces has deepened humanitarian tragedies, with rare earth mineral extraction fueling regional logistics networks. In Somalia, the complex security transition from ATMIS to AUSSOM in Somalia, combined with domestic friction over constitutional reform and resource distribution, continues to provide fertile ground for Al-Shabaab’s insurgency, resonating across the wider Red Sea space. Further south, the conflict in Cabo Delgado, Mozambique, has mutated into an elusive rural insurgency where local perceptions of economic exclusion around liquefied natural gas projects threaten to re-ignite communal grievances. Accounting for roughly 55 percent of all conflict-related fatalities on the continent, the Sahel remains Africa’s most volatile security theater, where the withdrawal of Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger from ECOWAS to form the Alliance of Sahel States has dismantled regional coordination, creating security vacuums exploited by jihadist groups. Compounding this instability is a profound technological shift in warfare: the proliferation of commercial and military drones by state and non-state actors across at least nine African countries for reconnaissance, explosive attacks, and online propaganda, cheapening the cost of conflict while exponentially increasing civilian casualties. Moving beyond traditional military paradigms, the 2026 Tana Forum dedicated substantial deliberation to the structural economic traps that underpin continental instability, with panelists and working papers arguing forcefully that security cannot be achieved in an economic vacuum. Delegates dissected the enduring legacy of extractive enclave economies, where African nations export critical raw materials while capturing virtually none of the value-addition, processing revenues, or industrial capabilities. This structural dependency, compounded by heavy debt burdens, unfavorable global trade terms, and reliance on third-party currencies for trade settlement, drains foreign reserves and starves domestic productive sectors of credit. Presenters called for a holistic redefinition of resource sovereignty, arguing that true sovereignty requires exercising total agency across the entire financial and industrial circuit, from local mineral processing and transparent resource-backed lending to domestic invoicing and strengthening intra-African trade channels anchored by the African Continental Free Trade Area. Parallel sessions on the continent’s severe energy deficit, where roughly 600 million Africans still lack reliable electricity, emphasized that regional power integration and transboundary energy pools are indispensable prerequisites for industrialization and sustainable peace. In an era where geopolitical competition has migrated into cyberspace, the forum issued sharp warnings regarding Africa’s digital vulnerability, stressing that digitalization cannot be treated merely as a matter of basic connectivity or technological modernization. When data ecosystems, cloud systems, algorithms, and artificial intelligence are owned and governed externally, African economies risk falling into a modern trap of digital imperialism, prompting experts to demand that African institutions build domestic capabilities in data governance, computing infrastructure, algorithmic transparency, and local software authorship to foster genuine economic independence. Another core pillar of the summit was the complex intersection between regional integration, informal markets, and transnational illicit economies. While the African Union champions regional integration as a vital economic and peace-building tool, the forum acknowledged that formal trade policies alone cannot overcome the realities on the ground, given that a massive share of Africa’s employment and economic activity occurs within the informal sector, functioning as a vital form of bottom-up integration that sustains vulnerable populations across porous borders. However, a critical analytical distinction was drawn between benign informality and destructive illicit economies, noting that while informal cross-border trade provides essential livelihoods, transnational illicit networks, including arms trafficking, environmental plunder, and large-scale trade mis-invoicing by corporate actors, actively fund armed insurgencies and undermine state authority. Empirical papers presented at the forum demonstrated that illicit financial flows are highly adaptive, persisting across fiscal years through entrenched institutional networks, leading delegates to conclude that security and economic integration must go hand in hand, replacing enforcement-only crackdowns with gradual formalization, stronger customs oversight, and the dismantling of high-level illicit financial circuits. As the three-day summit drew to its conclusion, delegates confronted the ultimate, recurring question that haunts high-level diplomatic convenings regarding whether the recommendations emerging from the Tana Forum are legally binding policy mandates or merely an elite agenda-setting platform. The institutional reality is clear. The Tana Forum possesses no direct enforcement mechanism, and its true power lies in its unique, informal character modeled after the traditional African baobab tree, serving as a candid intellectual incubator where sitting leaders, former heads of state, civil society actors, and researchers can speak frankly outside rigid diplomatic protocols. Yet, as Tana Board Chairperson and former Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama bluntly warned in his powerful closing address, the era of endless dialogue must yield to concrete implementation if the forum is to retain its credibility, asserting that it is good to talk and dialogue, but far better to act. Concluding the summit with a direct appeal for continental transformation, Mahama urged leaders “Let us return to Bahirdar next year and say that the tide is turning for Africa, that our conflicts are ending, and opportunities are being created for all our people.” To transform continental agency from a political slogan into tangible reality, the forum’s final recommendations mapped out a rigorous path forward, including granting Regional Economic Communities predictable and multi-year institutional funding rather than leaving them at the mercy of short-term donor whims when deploying peace support operations. Presenters also emphasized the necessity of institutionalizing public accountability by establishing transparent tracking mechanisms, such as public publication of treaty-ratification statuses, independent performance assessments of early-warning systems, and granting parliaments and media access to continental security data to ensure governments honor their commitments. Furthermore, researchers and panelists stressed the urgency of bridging the dangerous gap between detecting security risks and mobilizing rapid institutional responses before local disputes cascade into full-scale regional wars, while ensuring that formal peace agreements integrate economic restructuring, equitable resource-sharing, and local benefit thresholds to make peace structurally more profitable than war for conflict protagonists. Backdropped by the eternal, life-giving flow of the Blue Nile in Bahirdar, the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa delivered a stark, uncompromising message. Whether confronting Ethiopia’s bold geopolitical push for maritime access, managing the devastating resource-driven fragmentation of Sudan and the Sahel, or building robust economic and digital sovereignty, Africa’s path to sustainable peace requires moving past rhetorical posturing into disciplined, unified action. The intellectual framework has been laid bare by scholars, leaders, and security chiefs alike, and whether African governance structures possess the political discipline and institutional courage to translate these recommendations into hard policy remains the ultimate, defining test for the continent’s future. Drawing on the Forum recommendations, mainstreaming and working on the implementation part; takes African governments, international partners, regional and continental organizations renewing their commitments, actionable plans. The Prime Minister described the move as a significant milestone in Ethiopia’s efforts to strengthen its national defense and security capabilities. In a social media post, PM Abiy said Ethiopia’s comprehensive efforts to sustainably ensure peace and security had reached a new milestone. He added that the growing readiness of the country’s defense forces was enhancing its ability to deter potential aggression. “Today, in accordance with our prior agreement with the Russian government, we have taken delivery of the first twelve Su-35 4++ Generation fighter jets,” he said, adding that Ethiopia would also receive four S-400 air defense system batteries. Prime Minister Abiy expressed gratitude to Russian President Vladimir Putin for facilitating the delivery of the fighter jets a year ahead of the agreed schedule. He said the acquisition places Ethiopia at the forefront of Sub-Saharan African nations in equipping itself with the advanced fighter jets. The Prime Minister further elaborated that the development further strengthens Ethiopia’s sovereignty and enhances its defense capabilities, enabling the country to pursue its national security objectives while contributing to regional stability. The announcement comes as Prime Minister Abiy arrives in Moscow, Russia, to attend the Third Russia–Africa Summit, providing an opportunity to advance Ethiopia’s engagement with Russia and other African nations. The Prime Minister described the acquisition as a significant boost to Ethiopia’s collective security and its long-term efforts to safeguard national sovereignty and regional peace. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden

ethiopia.content: The Red Sea Chokehold: Why Maritime Access Is an Existential Question for Ethiopia – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-31 The Red Sea Chokehold: Why Maritime Access Is an Existential Question for Ethiopia 0 Comments For a landlocked nation, maritime access is rarely a matter of simple commerce; it is an existential variable that dictates economic survival, sovereign autonomy, and strategic viability. When a country’s geographic bottleneck is policed by a deeply militarized dictator with no clear economic vision, the resulting friction transcends ordinary bilateral disputes, elevating infrastructure into a primary casus belli. No regional dynamic illustrates this geopolitical chokehold more acutely than the volatile relationship between Ethiopia and Eritrea. For decades, international observers have viewed Ethiopia’s quest for a seaport through a purely commercial lens, equating it as a matter of trade balances, shipping tariffs, and economic optimization. But as the Red Sea rapidly transforms into one of the most volatile, hyper-militarized maritime corridors on the planet, this perspective is dangerously obsolete. For Ethiopia, a nation of over 130 million people, permanent and reliable access to the sea is no longer just an economic aspiration. It is an existential imperative for national security and survival. This assertion makes sense if viewed critically beyond a shallow attempt to reduce the looming danger to a simple expansionist ambition. One must always reconsider the facts on the ground while analyzing the conundrum in the Horn of Africa. Ethiopia, a country that is only 60 kms from the Red sea, is the most populous landlocked country in the world, whose significant portion of the population is youth and in active pursuit of job opportunities. According to recent IMF reports, the country is also home to the fastest growing economy in the entire sub-Saharan Africa. This is not merely a statistical trivia point framed for political purpose; rather it is a profound strategic vulnerability. Every piece of medicine, fuel, and technology that enters the country, and every single product exported to sustain its economy, depends entirely on the political whims and stability of its coastal neighbors. Currently, Ethiopia relies on Djibouti for roughly 95% of its trade, paying upwards between $1.5 to $2 billion annually in port fees. This single door dependency is an economic chokehold. No sovereign state can safely anchor its future on a single corridor that is vulnerable to external influences. For countries like Ethiopia, the highly volatile security situation in its surrounding doubles down the impact, without mentioning the challenges associated with the growing number of military bases in the region. Should political instability or hostile foreign influence freeze the docks of Djibouti, the Ethiopian economy would collapse triggering an internal humanitarian catastrophe of unprecedented scale. This is what makes Ethiopia’s concern undeniably legitimate and fuels its determination to address what it perceives as an existential threat through any means available. Just as a drowning person instinctively tries every possible option to stay afloat. A nation of 130 million people cannot be trapped in a geographic cage at the mercy of volatile, highly militarized autocratic coastal regime. A stable, secure Horn of Africa is impossible if its largest engine of population and economic powerhouse is kept in a state of permanent anxiety and artificial suffocation. Securing a permanent and dependable commercial and naval gateway to the Red Sea is not an empire building ambition or a luxury. For Ethiopia, it is becoming a simple, legitimate right to breath and it is the only way to bring peace and security in the entire Horn. Encirclement, Exclusion, and Ethiopia’s Security Imperative The urgency underpinning Ethiopia’s vulnerability has been sharply accelerated by the growing securitization of the Red Sea. What was once an open global trade route has become an arena for geopolitical chess, dominated by state coalitions and non-state actors from near and afar. Global and regional powers increasingly framing the vital corridor as a critical national security priority rather than just a commercial shipping lane. Driven by the need to safeguard chokepoints like the Bab el Mandab Strait from asymmetric threats, piracy, and regional conflicts, world powers have rapidly expanded their footprint through a dense concentration of military bases along the coastline. Djibouti has become the primary epicenter of this militarization, uniquely hosting overlapping naval facilities for both the United States (Camp Lemonnier) and China, alongside presence from France and Japan. Concurrently, nations like Russia have sought access, while regional actors such as Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Turkye, and Israel are all vying for influence via port logistics and security pacts along the broader Horn of Africa. While these external militaries provide short-term protection for international shipping, their crowding presence has ultimately transformed the Red Sea into a complex arena of overlapping geopolitical rivalries and proxy vulnerabilities, weakening the prospects for a self-sustaining regional security framework and brutally doubling down on Ethiopia’s unique vulnerability. As if these threats are not enough, Ethiopia is alarmed by a recent development of an architectural web of alliances orchestrated explicitly to isolate it from its own geographic backyard. The creation of the El Alamein Joint Declaration by Egypt, Eritrea, and Somalia is not as a routine diplomatic pact, but a deliberate strategy of encirclement. By codifying that Red Sea governance belongs exclusively to coastal states, regional adversaries seek to permanently deny landlocked Ethiopia a seat at the table. Proofing that the danger felt by Ethiopia is eminent beyond perception and this could potentially leave the country to consider every option to break the chokehold before it is too late. The action Ethiopia should take would be determined based on the scale and level of threats the country is faced with, as the end justifies the means. This encirclement is amplified by Egypt’s aggressive forward deployment rhetoric in the region. Driven by tensions over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), Cairo is trying to weaponize Ethiopia’s landlocked status by forming tight military and logistical alliances with Eritrea and other states bordering Ethiopia. From the Ethiopian perspective, it is quite clear. Hostile foreign militaries are aspiring to setting up base camps right on its borders, holding the keys to the very maritime gates that feed the Ethiopian population. This is a recuring dangerous move. Previously, when multinational coalitions form to protect Red Sea shipping lines from asymmetric threats like piracy and militant groups, Ethiopia is routinely excluded. Addis Ababa is being forced to watch from the sidelines while its primary economic lifeblood is policed by an alliance sympathetic to its rivals. It is profoundly naïve to expect Ethiopia to remain passive while such a perilous scheme is being orchestrated to threaten the lives of its entire population and its very survival. This reality underscores Ethiopia’s existential need to secure a reliable maritime corridor through which it can establish dependable port services and maintain a sovereign naval capability. Such a capability is essential to safeguard its national interests, protect its flag-bearing vessels, and guarantee its unhindered right to innocent passage under international law. Ethiopia has consistently expressed its preference for cooperation and has repeatedly advanced frameworks centered on mutual economic integration, shared prosperity, and regional interdependence. However, while Ethiopia remains committed to peaceful collaboration, coastal states, particularly Eritrea, should recognize that legal technicalities or strategies aimed at regional containment cannot serve as sustainable solutions to a matter that directly concerns the livelihood, security, and future of such burgeoning population. When the survival and long-term interests of the entire nation is at stake, it is unrealistic to expect Ethiopia to remain passive. It will undoubtedly pursue all the necessary strategic measures to secure its legitimate access to the Red Sea and protect its vital national interests. In doing so, it will ensure that its sovereignty, security, and economic future are safeguarded both on land and at sea. In conclusion, Ethiopia’s demand for access to the sea must be understood by its neighbouring countries as a legitimate strategic and economic and security concerns that deserves serious, constructive, and peaceful consideration. Why would Ethiopia’s quest to establish a military base along the Red Sea coast be considered unacceptable when countries from far beyond the region already maintain military bases and enjoy strategic access to the same coastline? Is it just to deny a neighbouring country with vital security and economic interests in the region an opportunity to negotiate such access, while external powers are permitted to establish a military presence there? The issue should not be approached through double standards or geopolitical rivalries, but through constructive dialogue, mutual respect, and negotiated arrangements that uphold the sovereignty of coastal states while addressing Ethiopia’s legitimate interests. IGAD and the African Union must urgently take their leadership responsibilities by facilitating inclusive regional dialogue and developing a practical framework that addresses Ethiopia’s legitimate aspirations while safeguarding the legitimate interests of neighbouring states. External actors outside the Horn of Africa should be discouraged from pursuing their agendas by fostering hostility and division, rather than promoting cooperation, dialogue, and regional stability. The international community, including the United Nations and other influential partners, should also intensify diplomatic engagement and support a negotiated settlement before the situation deteriorates into a dangerous confrontation with far reaching consequences for the Horn of Africa and beyond. The time to act is now: through timely diplomacy, mutual understanding, and political courage, regional leaders and international stakeholders can transform a potential source of conflict into an opportunity for cooperation, shared prosperity, and lasting peace. Failure to act decisively today risks allowing tensions to spiral into a devastating conflict that the region and the wider world can ill afford.
